title: API failure playbook drafts: timeouts, 429s, degraded streaming, error-rate spikes
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a living draft of SRE playbooks for the most common API failure modes we see in Redwood hosted endpoints: request timeouts, 429 (rate-limited) storms, degraded streaming (partial or very slow chunks), and elevated error-rate spikes (5xx/4xx anomalies). The intent is to give on-call engineers fast, ordered actions to stabilize user-facing traffic, collect evidence for RCA, and document mitigations and follow-ups.

Scope & assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood hosted API traffic (public REST + streaming websockets) and to the routing layer that fronts Dedicated/Private but not to customer VPC private ingress.
- Assumes on-call has access to: SRE PagerDuty, infra console, Grafana dashboards (api-latency, token-costs, streaming-chunks, envoy-stats), Kibana/Logs, kubectl to clusters, Redis/Rate-limiter dashboards, and the Redwood Console fallback controls.
- Quick wins prioritized over deep fixes during an active incident.

Triage checklist (first 5 minutes):
1) Confirm alert and scope
   - Which alert fired? (pager/system): e.g., API-5xx-spike-prod, API-99p-latency-prod, Streaming-error-rate
   - Check Grafana top-level: region, route, and model. Is it global or confined to one region/route/model?
2) Look for correlated signals
   - Latency heatmap, p50/p95/p99: are slow tails growing or entire distribution shifts?
   - Error breakdown: 5xx vs 4xx vs gateway timeouts (504) vs upstream timeouts (524)
   - Envoy/proxy stats: upstream_5xx, upstream_request_timeout, downstream_rq_429
   - Rate-limiter (Redis/hot keys) saturation: #blocked vs #allowed
3) Apply immediate mitigations (pick one or more depending on failure):
   - Enable emergency fallback route (route -> smaller model or cached response) for critical endpoints via Redwood Console rollout controls.
   - If streaming is degraded, flip to non-streaming endpoint for a short window for new requests (if product allows).
   - If 429s are dominant, temporarily increase rate-limit quota for internal health-checks only; avoid permissive global increases without approvals.
4) Communication
   - Post incident channel in Slack under #incidents-prod with short summary, impact, and who is on it.
   - Update PagerDuty incident with status and timeline.

Detection signatures & immediate actions by failure mode:

A) Timeouts (client-observed timeouts / 504 gateway timeouts)
Detection signals:
- Surge in 504/524 logs in API gateway and Envoy upstream timeout counters.
- P99 request latency rising sharply while p50 remains relatively steady (indicates heavy tail).
- Worker or GPU node metrics: CPU/RAM fine but worker thread pools saturated; increased queue lengths.
Immediate mitigations:
1) Reduce incoming work: add a temporary reject-or-shed policy for non-critical routes (use Gateway route config) or enable traffic shaping to slow new sessions.
2) Shorten upstream timeouts at gateway to fail fast (careful: this may increase 504s briefly but helps recover resources).
3) Drain and restart suspect worker pods: kubectl -n inference rollout restart deployment/<route-deployment> (target a small subset first).
4) Scale horizontally: if autoscaler is healthy, check why it didn’t scale (inspect HPA/KA, cluster node capacity). Temporarily increase replicas if safe.
Checks/commands:
- kubectl -n inference get pods -o wide --selector=route=<route>
- kubectl logs <pod> -c worker --since=10m | tail -n 200
- kubectl exec -it <pod> -c worker -- pstack /proc/$(pgrep worker)/stack (or use strace) if stuck threads suspected
- curl -v --max-time 15 https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate?route=<route> (to repro from internal network)
Notes:
- If underlying GPUs are saturated and queue latency is the cause, consider temporarily redirecting some traffic to lower-cost / lower-accuracy variants (routing policy fallback).

B) 429 storms (rate-limit enforcement)
Detection signals:
- Spike in downstream_rq_429 in Envoy and many clients reporting 429s; rate-limiter cache (Redis) showing hot key evictions or blocked requests counter rising.
- Suddenly high number of distinct client keys or concentrated traffic from a small number of API keys.
Immediate mitigations:
1) Identify offending key(s): query logs for top-api-key by request count last 10m. If a single key is noisy, throttle it or rotate its key.
2) Temporary emergency quota bump for essential customers only — apply via internal rate-limit admin UI with audit log.
3) For broad client-side retry storms, enable backoff header guidance and turn on 429 smoothing at gateway (limit token-bucket refill smoothing).
4) If rate-limiter Redis is saturated, fail-open policy for short window (only with approval from SRE lead) to reduce cascade.
Checks/commands:
- redis-cli -h <rate-limiter-host> INFO keyspace
- Query logs: kibana query: service:api AND status:429 | top(api_key)
- Rate-limiter dashboard: latency, blocked_count, memory-usage
Notes:
- Avoid wholesale increases to global rate-limits; prioritize targeted key actions and config changes with TTLs.

C) Degraded streaming (slow or incomplete chunks)
Detection signals:
- Streaming chunk interval (ms) metric increases, clients report partial responses or long gaps between SSE/WS frames.
- Proxy upstream flush patterns show slow socket writes or TLS renegotiations.
- Worker GC pauses or networking flakiness between inference nodes and gateway.
Immediate mitigations:
1) Switch new traffic to non-streaming endpoints (if product acceptable). Announce in status.
2) Toggle smaller chunk-size threshold in streaming gateway to force more frequent flushes temporarily.
3) Check for Nagle or socket-level buffering issues on edge proxies; inspect Envoy flush timers.
4) Redeploy streaming gateway if only gateway shows problem: kubectl rollout restart deployment/streaming-gateway -n infra
Checks/commands:
- Grafana: streaming-chunk-interval, streaming-bytes/sec, streaming-connection-errors
- tcpdump on gateway node (capture brief windows) to inspect packet timings
- kubectl logs gateway-pod -c envoy --since=15m | grep flush | tail -n 200
Notes:
- Streaming issues can be client-implementation sensitive (e.g., Chrome vs curl). When possible reproduce with a small script to isolate server vs client.

D) Elevated error rates (5xx or unusual 4xx patterns)
Detection signals:
- Sudden increase in 5xx across many routes or targeted on a service (model server, tokenization, or request-validation).
- Error messages in logs pointing to upstream service failure (e.g., model-serving: OOM, segfault, rate limiter errors).
Immediate mitigations:
1) Identify top failing service via traces and logs. Isolate by shutting down or circuit-breaking a failing dependency (e.g., model container).
2) Rollback recent deployments if correlated with deploy window (kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=<rev>).
3) If errors arise from a specific model version, route to previous pinned model.
4) If due to resource exhaustion, scale cluster nodes or evict noncritical workloads.
Checks/commands:
- kubectl get events -n inference --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -n 200
- kubectl describe pod <pod> -n inference
- Check OOMKill: journalctl -k | grep -i oom

Escalation & ownership:
- Primary on-call (SRE) owns initial mitigation. If model-serving appears root cause, escalate to applied-ml / serving-runtime oncall with tag @serving-runtime-oncall.
- If cluster-level resource limit is root cause, escalate to platform-engineering pager.
- For customer-impacting 429s or quota errors, loop in CS and account-owner via the incident channel.

Data collection checklist (during incident):
- Capture Grafana links and screenshots for key dashboards.
- Save representative logs: kubectl logs <pod> --since=30m > /tmp/pod-logs.txt
- Create a support bundle: /scripts/gather-support-bundle.sh --namespace inference --since 30m
- Save a lightweight trace for a failing request (x-trace headers).

Short-term post-incident tasks (first 48 hours):
- Restore normal routing and rate-limits with documented change windows.
- Open ticket for RCA: tag engineers who made mitigation changes.
- Run hit-replay of affected traffic subset in staging to reproduce.

RCA and long-term mitigations (example categories):
- Autoscaler tuning: adjust HPA/KA thresholds, add proactive scale-up during expected bursts.
- Circuit breakers: add finer-grained CBs per route/model with quick-fail instead of slow tail buildup.
- Rate-limiter improvements: hot-key protection and more visible per-key dashboards.
- Streaming resilience: add client keepalive pings and server-side heartbeat monitoring.
- Observability: add alert for growing queue_length / worker_queue_latency before p99 latency spike.

Post-incident playback checklist:
1) Confirm all mitigations reverted and documented with timestamps.
2) Author RCA with timeline, root cause hypothesis, evidence, impact, and action items. Add links to logs and support bundle.
3) Assign owners and SLAs for action items.
4) Communicate summary to stakeholders and update status page if public incident.

Runbook TODOs (draft items to complete):
- Add exact kubectl/helm commands for each deployment to reduce ambiguity in playbook steps. (owner: Liam)
- Harden scripted emergency fallback that toggles route -> cached response with one click. (owner: Priya)
- Add runbook snippet to safely fail-open the rate-limiter with audit trail and TTL. (owner: Diego)
- Add runbook automation: self-heal candidate that drains/restarts > 10% of failing pods. (owner: Hannah)
- Create replay harness for suspect traffic shapes and add to CI. (owner: eng-sre)

Notes & gotchas from past incidents:
- During the 2025-10 spike, raising gateway timeouts increased tail latency because upstream GPU queues grew; subsequent fix was to add circuit-breakers.
- A 429 storm in 2024 was traced to SDK clients that aggressively retried without jitter — consider adding guidance and baked-in client headers.
- Streaming regressions are often due to small config drifts in Envoy flush timers when we deploy sidecars — always snapshot envoy.yaml before deploy.

Contact & escalation list:
- SRE oncall: @sre-oncall (PagerDuty)
- Serving runtime oncall: @serving-runtime-oncall
- Platform eng: @platform-oncall
- PS / Solutions engineering (for high-touch customer work): @solutions-eng

Revision history:
- 2025-11-03: initial draft (Maya Chen)
- 2026-01-08: added streaming checklist and commands (Priya Nair)
- 2026-03-13: updated detection signals and TODOs (Maya Chen)

Appendix: useful queries and snippets
- Top erroring routes (Kibana): service:api AND level:error | top(route)
- Top keys by requests (Kibana): service:api AND @timestamp:>now-10m | stats count by api_key | sort -count
- Quick pod restart pattern: kubectl -n inference rollout restart deployment/<deployment> --grace-period=30 && watch kubectl get pods -n inference --selector=route=<route>

End of draft.

(Keep this file light and prescriptive; link to detailed Confluence pages for deeper RCA writeups.)
